ai-and-the-job: Watch a job decompose. The role is product manager, but it could be anyone. Each task gets a label. Some are human-only — judgement calls, context, accountability. Some pair the human with AI for speed. A few become AI-only — boilerplate, lookups. The role then re-stacks. Same title, different mix inside. The job didn't disappear. It got redrawn.
trap-ai-and-the-job: Here's the trap. A leader announces, AI replaces this role. Layoffs follow. But the strategic, judgement, and accountability tasks were never automatable. Three months later, those tasks come back as five different contractor invoices. The fix? Decompose the role first. Tag each task. Then automate, augment, or keep — task by task, not job by job.
team-design-with-ai: Three patterns. Pattern A — human does everything, AI watches. Slow. Pattern B — AI drafts, human reviews. Faster, but trust handoff is fuzzy. Pattern C — AI executes within a tight contract, human owns the contract and the failure mode. Watch the work move. Watch the failure mode move with it. The leader's job is choosing which pattern fits which workflow.
trap-team-design-with-ai: The trap is hidden hand-off. Manager assumes AI checked the figures. Analyst assumes manager will. Customer gets the wrong number. Nobody owns the gap. Fix it by writing the contract — exactly which step is human, which is AI, and who catches what when something breaks.
talent-and-hiring: Two candidates, same task. Candidate A executes the AI's draft faster than anyone in the room. Candidate B reads it slowly, spots the hallucinated citation, sends it back. Six months later — A is shipping rework. B is shipping. In an AI-augmented team, judgement scales. Execution speed without judgement is just faster errors.
trap-talent-and-hiring: The trap is hiring for AI fluency alone. The candidate uses every tool. Their portfolio is dazzling. But ask, what would you not let AI do here? They can't answer. Six months later they ship a confident wrong number to the board. Hire for taste, judgement, and the ability to say no — even when AI is sure.
learning-and-development: AI tooling knowledge has a six-week half-life. Watch the annual training calendar against that clock. The first cohort learned a workflow that no longer exists. The compounding leader runs sprint-cadence learning instead — small experiments, weekly demos, a real artifact every two weeks. The half-life isn't going to slow down for your training calendar.
trap-learning-and-development: The trap is annual training. You scheduled it nine months ago for the tools your team needed then. The tools have changed three times since. Half the room is rolling their eyes. The fix — replace the annual day with a weekly thirty-minute show-and-tell. Whatever's new, someone demos. Learning speed becomes a leadership KPI.
ethics-and-trust: Trust compounds — slowly. Each time behaviour matches stated values, the line goes up a little. Each time it doesn't, it crashes. AI deployment is the highest-stakes consistency test most companies will face. The boring hard work is choosing what AI will not do, even when it could, because your stated values demand it. Then never breaking that line.
trap-ethics-and-trust: The trap is the ethics page. Your company published one. It's beautiful. Then a single shipped AI feature contradicts it — surveillance, dark pattern, manipulative copy. The page now reads as a lie. Trust crashes overnight. The fix — every AI launch goes through one question. Does this match what we said we'd do? If not, it doesn't ship.
